title: Instructing Students on Effective Sequences of Examples and Problems https://psycnet.apa.org/record/2021-70435-001 nd-problems/
author: Barton, Craig
source: Tips for Teachers (tipsforteachers.co.uk), December 18, 2024 — original paper:
summary: This entry covers a study by van Harsel and colleagues testing how well college students self-regulate their learning of problem-solving skills when given free choice between worked examples and practice problems in an online environment. The researchers compared task-selection patterns across three conditions: self-regulated learning with instructional guidance on effective strategies, self-regulated learning without such guidance, and a fixed, teacher-sequenced condition. The headline finding is that students were surprisingly competent at choosing effective learning tasks on their own, even without being taught the underlying principles of good sequencing, though there was still room for improvement. Barton frames this as evidence that student choice in self-regulated environments can work reasonably well, while also flagging that explicit instruction in evidence-based task-selection strategies could push performance further. The study calls for more research into which circumstances support or undermine students' capacity to regulate their own learning of examples and problems.
points: College students given free choice between worked examples and practice problems were relatively good at self-regulating their task selection, even without explicit strategy instruction.
Explicit instruction in evidence-based task-selection principles may still improve students' choices further, since some room for improvement remained.
Self-regulated learning conditions can rival fixed-sequence instruction for motivation and learning outcomes in the right online contexts.
Teachers should consider building in practice and reflection opportunities so students can experience the benefits of planning their own learning strategy.
quotes: The findings suggest that the higher education students who participated in this study were relatively good at regulating their own learning with examples and problems in online learning environments
Higher education students appear to be quite good at regulating their own learning with examples and problems when allowed to choose their own learning tasks

Providing students with control over their own learning is becoming more common, especially in higher education. Allowing students to choose their own learning path can be effective and motivating for some student populations
There is still room for improvement in student task selection. Informing students about evidence-based instructional design principles may improve task selections
Teachers might consider incorporating opportunities for students to practice and reflect on the information provided to them
